dedupe_keys.name: hospital level urban flood risk and targeted adaptation for about 14 000 general hospitals in 337 chinese cities lancet public health 2026

description: This modelling study estimates how urban flooding will affect China's general hospitals as the climate warms and what targeted adaptation would cost. The PubMed abstract read on 2026-09-28, from a June 2026 Lancet Public Health article by Shangchen Zhang and colleagues at Tsinghua University and partner institutions, describes a national database of general hospitals built by the authors and an urban flood model driven by precipitation at 9 km and 15-minute resolution, used to estimate the maximum water depth at about 14,000 hospitals in 337 cities and the resulting direct losses and health impacts, with and without adaptation. Coverage is urban China to the 2080s. Under a medium warming scenario, even full adaptation to 2020 flood levels leaves annual hospital losses of 9.1 billion US dollars by the 2080s and delayed diagnoses for 6.8 million people, about half as much again under higher warming; a uniform national programme would cost 51 to 97 billion dollars to remove most losses, whereas city- and hospital-specific measures achieve similar results for 8 to 12 billion. The article is open access under CC BY-NC 4.0. Caveats: whether the hospital database and flood depths are released was not read, and the results rest on modelled rainfall and flood depths. It supports hospital flood adaptation planning, such as ranking hospitals for floodproofing budgets. Related record: China's 1-km hospital travel time and accessibility maps. Licence (read on 2026-09-29): CC-BY-NC-4.0 (article).

name: Hospital-level urban flood risk and targeted adaptation for about 14,000 general hospitals in 337 Chinese cities (Lancet Public Health 2026)
organisations: National Center for Climate Change Strategy and International Cooperation
outcomes: Under a medium warming scenario, even with full adaptation to 2020 flooding levels, annual direct flood losses in hospitals reach US$9.1 billion by the 2080s (6.9% of China's 2022 government medical insurance spending) with delayed diagnoses for 6.8 million people, about 50% more under higher warming; a uniform national adaptation strategy would cost US$51.2-97.4 billion to bring losses near zero, while city- and hospital-specific strategies achieve similar results for US$8.2-11.9 billion.
provider: Shangchen Zhang, W. Cai, P. Gong and co-authors (Tsinghua University and partners), The Lancet Public Health
resources_used: national database of general hospitals built by the authors
precipitation data at 9 km and 15 min resolution
